docs.title: NFC Key Management
docs.text: How the AES-256 keys that encrypt NFC chip payloads are configured, rotated and retired. Until now these rules lived only in pull request descriptions; this is the reference.

docs.title: 1. What the keys protect
docs.text:
Every HWB chip — a patient bracelet or a guardian card — carries its clinical payload encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The key comes from the backend at login and is held by the device so it can read and write chips offline, which is the whole point: brigades work without connectivity.

The chip is a cache, not the source of truth. Its hardware UID is unencrypted and always readable, so a device with connectivity can always resolve the patient from the backend even when it cannot decrypt the payload.

docs.title: 2. The keyring
docs.text:
There is not one key but a keyring: a map of version -> key. The backend delivers the whole ring at login, refresh and /users/me. Devices decrypt with whichever version a chip names and encrypt with the current one.

Setting Meaning NFC_MASTER_KEY The original key. Registered as version 0. NFC_KEY_V<n> The key for version n. One environment variable per key. NFC_CURRENT_KEY_VERSION The version new writes are encrypted with. Defaults to 0.

Every key must be exactly 64 hexadecimal characters (32 bytes) and every version must be between 0 and 255 — the version travels in a single byte of the payload header.

The application refuses to start if any key is malformed or if NFC_CURRENT_KEY_VERSION has no matching key. The error names the offending variable and never prints its value. A deployment with no NFC key at all is valid; NFC is simply unavailable.

docs.title: Wire format
docs.text:
version 0 : [12-byte nonce][ciphertext][16-byte tag]
version 1+: ['H']['W'][version][nonce][ciphertext][tag]
            with the three header bytes authenticated as associated data

Version 0 deliberately writes the pre-versioning layout so an older build can still read chips written by a newer one during a partial rollout.

docs.title: 3. Field history
docs.text:
Recorded so the state of chips already in circulation is not guesswork.

Every chip written in the field to date is key version 0, in the headerless format. No build carrying the versioned wire format was distributed to any device between 3 and 8 September 2026, so nothing was ever written with a version header, and no rotation has taken place: NFC_CURRENT_KEY_VERSION has been 0 throughout.

That means the two formats never coexisted in the field, and the wire format is frozen from the current build onwards. It also means the key in NFC_MASTER_KEY is the only key any existing chip can be read with — losing or changing it makes every chip in circulation unreadable offline.

docs.title: 4. Generating a key
docs.text:
openssl rand -hex 32

Store it in Secret Manager. Never commit a real key, and never paste one into an issue or a chat.

docs.title: 5. Rotating
docs.text:
Rotation limits how long a leaked key stays useful. It does not re-encrypt existing chips: those migrate when they are next written.

  1. Generate a new key and create a new secret, e.g. hwb-nfc-key-v1.
  2. Mount it in cloudbuild.yaml under --update-secrets as NFC_KEY_V1.
  3. Set NFC_CURRENT_KEY_VERSION=1 under --update-env-vars.
  4. Deploy. New writes use version 1; version 0 stays in the ring for reading.

Never add a new version to an existing secret. NFC_MASTER_KEY is mounted as hwb-nfc-master-key:latest. Adding a Secret Manager version to that secret silently changes what version 0 is, and every existing chip becomes unreadable. Rotation always means a new secret with a new name.

Do not set NFC_CURRENT_KEY_VERSION above 0 until every device runs a build that understands the keyring. An older build takes the current key and ignores the ring, losing the ability to read anything written under the old key.

docs.title: Migration is passive
docs.text: A chip moves to the current version when something rewrites it — a consultation, a vaccine, an edit. A read alone does not migrate it. Chips belonging to people who never return stay on their original version indefinitely.

docs.title: 6. Retiring a version
docs.text:
Retiring means removing NFC_KEY_V<n> from the deployment. From that moment, chips still on version n cannot be decrypted offline.

They are not lost: with connectivity the UID still resolves the patient from the backend, and the next write migrates the chip. The degradation is "this chip is online-only until someone uses it once with a signal".

docs.title: Telemetry storage
docs.text:
Sightings land in nfc_key_version_observations, created by scripts/create_tables.py like every other table. It is append-only: the device keeps one row per chip, the server keeps every sighting, because the gap between consecutive sightings of the same UID is what a retention period has to be sized from.

observed_at must arrive with a timezone offset. A naive value would be read as UTC and silently shift the sighting by the reporting device's own offset, which corrupts ordering between devices in different zones. The API rejects naive timestamps.

Attribution ("latest sighting wins") is ordered by the server's clock, not the client's, so a device with a skewed clock cannot make a stale sighting outrank a newer one reported elsewhere.

docs.title: Check before retiring
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/patients/nfc-key-versions/usage?window_days=90

Requires org_admin or superadmin. It reports how many distinct chips were last seen on each version, split by patient and guardian, plus retirable_versions — versions with no sighting inside the window.

Read retirable_versions as a veto, not a clearance. A version missing from the telemetry may still have chips in the field whose patients have not come back. Absence of sightings is not evidence of absence of chips. It can tell you a retirement is obviously unsafe; it cannot tell you one is safe.

Watch the guardian rows specifically. Guardian cards are written with the same keyring but rewritten less often, so they are the likelier stragglers and a bracelet-only reading is optimistic.

docs.title: Retirement is manual today
docs.text: Nothing creates or retires versions automatically. Both are human actions requiring deploy access. This is a known limitation: a control that depends on someone remembering a periodic chore is weak, and it is worse for a self-hosting adopter who will not administer keys at all. Automating the lifecycle — and the retention policy it would need — remains open.

docs.title: 7. On the device
docs.text:
• The keyring lives in the platform secure store (Keystore / Keychain).
  • It is bounded by the session window: it is only served while the refresh token's exp is in the future, checked locally so it holds offline. Outside the window it is wiped from memory and disk and NFC is refused.
  • Moving the device clock backwards more than 24 hours is treated as tampering and closes the window. The high-water mark is re-anchored to the server's own clock (the refresh token's iat) on every successful login and refresh, so a device whose clock ran ahead recovers by reconnecting rather than staying locked out.
  • superadmin accounts receive no key material: they have no clinical access and never touch a chip.

docs.title: 8. Local development
docs.text:
NFC_KEY_V<n> entries are read from .env as well as from the process environment, so a rotation can be exercised locally:

NFC_MASTER_KEY="<64 hex chars>"
NFC_KEY_V1="<64 hex chars>"
NFC_CURRENT_KEY_VERSION=1

A real environment variable of the same name wins over the .env entry, matching every other setting. Use throwaway values locally — never a production key.

docs.title: Security Architecture & Protocols
docs.text: This document outlines the security measures, cryptographic standards, and access control models implemented in the Health Without Borders API. The system follows a "Defense in Depth" strategy, securing Protected Health Information (PHI) and Personally Identifiable Information (PII) at the application, transport, and storage levels.

docs.title: 1. Authentication (AuthN)
docs.text:
Authentication uses the OAuth2 Password Flow with JSON Web Tokens (JWT). The system implements a short-lived access token + long-lived refresh token pattern with JTI-based revocation.

  • Signing Algorithm: HS256 (HMAC with SHA-256) using a high-entropy SECRET_KEY injected at runtime.
  • Access Token: Short-lived (default 60 minutes, configurable via ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES). Used for every API call. Contains sub (user email), exp (expiration), jti (unique JWT ID for revocation), and type ("access"). No PHI or PII in the token.
  • Refresh Token: Longer-lived (default 7 days, configurable via REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES). Used only to obtain a new token pair via POST /login/refresh. Contains the same claims with type set to "refresh". The old refresh token is revoked on each rotation to prevent reuse.
  • Token Revocation: Tokens can be explicitly revoked via POST /logout. The jti claim is stored in the revoked_tokens database table and checked on every authenticated request. Revoked entries can be cleaned up after their original expiry passes.
  • Password Storage: Bcrypt iterative hashing. Plaintext passwords are never stored.

docs.title: 1.1. Token Flow
docs.text:
1. POST /login/access-token  →  { access_token, refresh_token, expires_in }
2. Use access_token in Authorization: Bearer header for all API calls
3. When access_token expires (401) → POST /login/refresh { refresh_token }
   → Returns new { access_token, refresh_token } (old refresh is revoked)
4. POST /logout  →  Revokes current access_token (204 No Content)

docs.title: 2. Authorization (AuthZ) & Multi-Tenancy
docs.text: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Tenant isolation applies to organization and user administration; patient clinical records are intentionally global — any authenticated clinician may access any patient (see Database Schema § 3.1).

docs.title: 2.1. System Roles
docs.text: Role Scope Capabilities superadmin Global Create organizations and provision org_admin users org_admin Organization Manage doctor and nurse accounts within their organization doctor Organization Full clinical access: read records, create patients, add medical history nurse Organization Restricted: read records, add vaccines. Cannot add medical history

docs.title: 2.2. Patient Authorization (Hardware 2FA)
docs.text:
For physical security in refugee or transit camps:

  • Adults (18+): Scanning the NFC tag retrieves the medical record.
  • Minors (<18): Access is blocked unless the guardian's NFC tag is also scanned and matches the registered guardian.

docs.title: 3.1. Encryption at Rest
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL on Google Cloud SQL encrypted with AES-256 (Google-managed keys).
  • NFC chip payloads encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a versioned keyring. See NFC Key Management for configuration, rotation and retirement.
  • Automated backups are identically encrypted.

docs.title: 3.2. Encryption in Transit
docs.text:
• External: TLS 1.3 (HTTPS) between mobile clients and Cloud Run.
  • Internal: Unix Sockets between Cloud Run and Cloud SQL.

docs.title: 3.3. Clinical Interoperability Security (FHIR)
docs.text: FHIR RDA bundles sent to the Google Cloud Healthcare API are protected by: - IAM Service Accounts: Scoped to roles/healthcare.fhirResourceEditor. - Cloud Audit Logs: Every bundle ingestion triggers an immutable audit log entry. - Referential Integrity: Enabled on the FHIR Store to prevent malformed references. - Resource Versioning: Enabled to maintain a complete audit trail of all changes.

docs.title: 4.1. Network Isolation
docs.text:
• Cloud SQL has no public IP — accessed via internal VPC routing or Unix sockets.
  • Cloud Run instances are ephemeral (no persistent attack surface).

docs.title: 4.2. Secret Management
docs.text:
• Sensitive configurations injected at runtime via Google Secret Manager.
  • No secrets committed to the Git repository.

docs.title: 4.3. Rate Limiting
docs.text:
API endpoints that are vulnerable to brute-force attacks (/login/access-token, /patients/search) enforce per-client request limits using SlowAPI.

  • Backend Storage: Redis (shared across all Cloud Run instances). Configured via the REDIS_URL environment variable. Falls back to in-memory storage for local development when REDIS_URL is not set.
  • Client IP Detection: Extracted from the X-Forwarded-For header set by Cloud Run's load balancer, ensuring rate limits apply per real client rather than per proxy.
  • Default Limits: 10/minute for login, 30/minute for patient search. Configurable via RATE_LIMIT_LOGIN and RATE_LIMIT_PATIENT_SEARCH environment variables.

docs.title: 5.1. Data Classification
docs.text: Category Examples Authentication (Sensitive) Emails, hashed passwords, roles, organization IDs PII Patient names, dates of birth, guardian names, document numbers PHI (Critical) Patient IDs, device UIDs, medical history, diagnoses (ICD-10/11), allergies, vaccinations

docs.title: 5.2. Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Origin: Tablet generates JSON payload (offline-first).
  2. Transit 1: Tablet → Backend via HTTPS (TLS 1.3).
  3. Processing: Cloud Run validates JWT/RBAC. Missing diagnoses inferred via Vertex AI (data NOT used for model training).
  4. Transit 2: Backend → PostgreSQL via Unix Sockets.
  5. Transit 3: Backend converts JSON to FHIR R4 RDA bundles → Cloud Healthcare API via HTTPS (GCP IAM).

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
This guide is for the healthcare staff who use the Health Without Borders mobile app in the field — during medical brigades and at pilot sites. It explains, step by step, how to register patients, read and update their records with NFC/QR bracelets, and keep everything synchronized.

No technical knowledge is required. If you are looking for API, architecture, or deployment documentation, see the Development and Infrastructure and Security sections instead.

docs.title: What the app does
docs.text:
Health Without Borders stores a patient's clinical record on an NFC/QR bracelet and keeps a synchronized copy on the server. Because brigades often work without a stable internet connection, the app is offline-first: you can register patients and record care with no signal, and the app will synchronize automatically when a connection is available.

A single patient has one shared record across all participating organizations, so any authenticated professional can read and update it at the point of care.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A mobile device with NFC enabled (Android) and the app installed.
  • Your login credentials, provided by your organization administrator.
  • Patient NFC bracelets and, when applicable, guardian cards.

Note: The interface is available in Spanish and English. You can switch the language at any time from the header (see Getting Started).

docs.title: How this guide is organized
docs.text:
1. Getting Started — Log in, understand the home screen, switch language, and sign out safely.
  2. Registering a New Patient — Create a patient, assign the bracelet, and add guardians.
  3. Finding & Viewing a Patient — Search, scan a bracelet, and read the clinical history.
  4. Consultations & Vaccines — Add care to a patient's record.
  5. Syncing Pending Records — Understand and clear the sync queue.
  6. Statistics — Review brigade activity (administrators).
  7. Administration — Manage users and organizations (administrators).

docs.title: Administration: Users & Organizations
docs.text: These screens are for administrators. They let you manage the people and organizations that use the platform.

docs.title: 1. Manage users
docs.text:
Open Manage users to see the users in your organization, grouped by role (for example, Administrator, Doctor, Nurse).

From a user's detail you can:

  • Create a new user.
  • Deactivate a user — the account is suspended but not removed.
  • Delete a user — the account is removed.

docs.title: 2. Manage organizations
docs.text:
Open Organizations to see the list of organizations. Selecting one opens its details (identifier, status, number of users, number of patients).

From an organization's detail you can:

  • Deactivate the organization.
  • Delete the organization.

Note: Deleting an organization protects patient records — patient data is never removed. Associated user accounts are deactivated together with the organization.

docs.title: 3. A note on roles
docs.text: What you can see and do depends on your role. Organization administrators act within their own organization; super administrators can act across organizations. If an option is not visible to you, your role does not include that permission.

docs.title: Consultations & Vaccines
docs.text: This page explains how to add clinical care — consultations and vaccines — to a patient's record.

docs.title: 1. Add a consultation
docs.text:
1. Open the patient's record (by scanning the bracelet or searching), or use the summary screen right after registration.
  2. Tap Add consultation.
  3. Complete the consultation details and save.

docs.title: 2. Add a vaccine
docs.text:
1. From the same summary or record screen, tap Add vaccine.
  2. Enter the vaccine information and save.

docs.title: 3. How the bracelet is updated
docs.text:
When you add a consultation or a vaccine, the bracelet is marked as modified so the new information is written back to the NFC chip and synchronized to the server. If you are offline, the change is stored locally and appears in the pending-to-sync queue until a connection is available.

Note: After adding care, use Finish to complete the encounter. Remember to write the bracelet if it is still marked as pending.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page covers logging in, the home screen, changing the language, and signing out safely.

docs.title: 1. Logging in
docs.text:
1. Open the app. On the login screen, enter the email and password provided by your organization administrator.
  2. Tap Log in.

Your access depends on your role (for example, medical staff, or an organization administrator). Administrators see additional options such as Statistics, Manage users, and Organizations.

Note: Once you are logged in, the app keeps your session active as you move between screens. If your session expires, you will be asked to sign in again — any records you registered in the field are kept on the device until they can be synchronized.

docs.title: 2. The home screen
docs.text:
From the home screen you can reach the main actions:

  • New patient — register a patient and assign a bracelet.
  • Search patients — find an existing patient.
  • Pending to sync — review records waiting to be uploaded. A gold badge shows the number of records still stored locally (including any duplicates or errors).

Administrators also see Statistics, Manage users, and Organizations.

docs.title: 3. Changing the language
docs.text:
The app is bilingual. Use the ES / EN switch in the header to change the language instantly — titles, buttons, filters, and cards update immediately, with no need to restart the screen. Dates are also shown in the format that matches the selected language.

The language switch is available on the main screens, including New patient, Search patients, Pending to sync, Manage users, and Organizations.

docs.title: 4. Signing out
docs.text:
1. Open the menu and tap Log out.
  2. If you have records pending synchronization, the confirmation dialog will warn you and recommend syncing before you leave. When possible, sync your pending records first so nothing is left only on the device.

docs.title: Finding & Viewing a Patient
docs.text: This page explains how to find an existing patient and how to read a patient's clinical record from their bracelet.

docs.title: 1. Search for a patient
docs.text:
1. From the home screen, tap Search patients.
  2. Enter the patient's identifying details (for example, document number or name).
  3. Tap Search.

If no match is found, the app shows the message: "No patient found with these details. Please check the fields." Review the values you entered and try again.

docs.title: 2. Read a patient by scanning the bracelet
docs.text:
At the point of care, the fastest way to open a record is to scan the patient's bracelet:

  1. Choose the read option and tap Start.
  2. Hold the patient's bracelet (or the guardian card) against the back of the phone.
  3. The patient's record opens once the bracelet is read.

Note: The bracelet identifier is unambiguous, so scanning always opens the correct patient. Manual search is best when the bracelet is unavailable.

docs.title: 3. Read the clinical record
docs.text:
When a record is open, the information is organized into tabs:

  • Summary — the patient's key information at a glance.
  • Consultations — the list of recorded consultations.
  • Vaccines — the vaccines registered for the patient.
  • Consultation details — the full detail of a selected consultation.

Dates are shown in the format that matches the selected language (ES / EN).

docs.title: 4. Emergency access
docs.text: In urgent situations, the app provides an emergency ("break-glass") access path so that care is never blocked. Every emergency access is recorded in an audit log (who accessed the record and when). Use it only when clinically necessary.

docs.title: Registering a New Patient
docs.text: This page explains how to create a new patient, assign the patient's NFC bracelet, and add one or two guardians.

docs.title: 1. Start a new registration
docs.text:
1. From the home screen, tap New patient.
  2. The registration form opens. You can switch the language (ES / EN) at any time from the header.

docs.title: 2. Enter the patient's information
docs.text:
Complete the fields in each section:

  • Patient NFC device — the identifier of the bracelet you will assign (you can also scan it in the next step).
  • Identification — document type, document number, first and last names (second name and second surname are optional).
  • Demographic data — date of birth and biological sex.
  • Nationality — choose from the list. If the nationality is not listed, select "Other".

Required fields are marked with an asterisk (). The Continue* button advances through the steps.

docs.title: 3. Assign the patient bracelet
docs.text:
When prompted, the app shows the guided writing screen ("Patient bracelet"):

  1. Tap Start.
  2. Hold the patient's bracelet against the back of the phone until the app confirms the write.

Note: You can tap Skip to finish the registration without writing the bracelet immediately. In that case the patient is saved locally and marked as "Pending to write to the NFC device", so you can write the bracelet later.

docs.title: 4. Add guardians
docs.text:
For patients who require a guardian, you can register up to two guardians:

  1. Enter each guardian's information.
  2. Capture the guardian's consent signature when requested.
  3. When prompted with the "Guardian card" screen, hold the guardian card against the phone to write it.

Note: The guardian's consent signature is preserved on the server; it is not lost when the guardian card is synchronized.

docs.title: 5. Finish and save
docs.text:
On the summary screen you can:

  • Add consultation or Add vaccine (see Consultations & Vaccines).
  • Tap Finish to complete the registration.

The patient is saved locally first and appears in the pending-to-sync queue until the app uploads it to the server.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: The Statistics screen gives administrators an overview of brigade activity — patients, vaccines, and nationalities. Availability depends on your role.

docs.title: 1. Access and scope
docs.text:
• Organization administrators see the statistics for their own organization.
  • Super administrators can see all organizations, or narrow the view to a single one using the organization dropdown.

You can switch the language (ES / EN) from the header.

docs.title: 2. Filter by period
docs.text:
Use the quick filter buttons to choose the time window:

  • All — all available data.
  • This month — the current month to date.
  • Last 20 days — a rolling recent window.
  • Custom — opens a calendar where you select a specific date range.

The figures and trends update to match the selected period, comparing it against the previous one where applicable.

docs.title: Syncing Pending Records
docs.text: Because the app is offline-first, records you create in the field are first saved on the device and then uploaded to the server. This page explains how to review and clear those pending records.

docs.title: 1. Why records are pending
docs.text: When there is no connection — or when a bracelet still needs to be written — new patients and updates are stored locally and queued for synchronization. The home screen shows a gold badge with the number of records still pending (including any duplicates or records with errors).

docs.title: 2. The sync queue
docs.text:
Open Pending to sync from the home screen. Each record is shown as a card with a clear status:

  • Pending — waiting to be uploaded.
  • Error — the upload did not complete; the card explains, in plain language, what to do.
  • Duplicate — the record matches one already on the server.

docs.title: 3. Synchronize
docs.text:
• Tap Sync now on a single record, or Sync all to upload the whole queue.
  • Tap Review to inspect a record before syncing.

When a record uploads successfully, it leaves the queue and the home badge count goes down.

Note: Technical system-error details are intentionally hidden from this screen to keep it clear. When you sign out, the app warns you if records are still pending — sync them first whenever possible so nothing is left only on the device.
